France welcomes the adoption of resolution 2467 (2019), a milestone rather than the end of our effort. The strengthened mandate for the Special Representative on Sexual Violence in Conflict, Ms. Pramila Patten, and a survivor-centred approach are important advances. The requested Secretary-General report on children born of rape by 2021 remains a request, not a completed report.

We criticize the removal of previously agreed sexual and reproductive health language under pressure from permanent members and veto threats. Victims need sexual and reproductive health care; the omission undermines women's dignity. Women must decide freely about their bodies, including choosing to terminate involuntary pregnancies.

Our position on full sexual and reproductive health care and rights in every context remains unchanged. We will continue to support and promote that approach in the Security Council, other UN bodies and elsewhere. Earlier health provisions—paragraph 19 of resolution 2106 (2013) and paragraph 10 of resolution 1889 (2009)—remain in the reaffirmed framework; their omission does not erase them.

This statement does not establish endorsement of an unspecified future text or a future vote. Our ongoing commitment to survivor health and rights is clear.<|im_end|>

output_raw:
The United Kingdom welcomes the adoption of resolution 2467 (2019), a German achievement, while noting defects. The survivor-centred approach remains a priority, yet more steps are needed for true justice and accountability. Conflict-related sexual violence disproportionately affects women and girls; civil society plays an important role. We regret the omission of language on services for survivors. That omission overlooks the acute need for comprehensive reproductive and sexual health care.

Access to such care is compatible with a survivor-centred approach. Our support for survivor access to sexual and reproductive health care around the world continues. These real commitments do not establish endorsement of an unspecified future text or a future vote. The hypothetical analytical recommendation to revise a survivor-centred proposal by providing immediate comprehensive sexual and reproductive care without a conviction gate, and to fund a survivor-referral route for care alongside a separate voluntary protected referral route for investigation and prosecution, is an exercise recommendation. It does not alter our established support for survivor access to sexual and reproductive health care.<|im_end|>
